lede: When a Spark job is slow, the first question is how the work was split up and who ran each piece. This lesson names the parts of a Spark application and lets you look at them on a real one.
objectives: Describe what the driver, the executors and the tasks each do
Explain how partitions become tasks, and how many run at once
Check where Spark runs and how parallel it is with `master` and `defaultParallelism`
Count a DataFrame's partitions, and change them with `repartition`

blocks.md:
Every Spark application has one **driver** and one or more **executors**.

- The **driver** runs your Python program. When you ask for a result, it plans the work, splits it into tasks, hands them out and gathers the answers.
- **Executors** are worker processes that run those tasks, each on its own cores.
- A **task** is the work for one partition. A step over a DataFrame with 6 partitions becomes 6 tasks. With 2 cores, 2 tasks run at a time and the rest wait their turn.

On a **cluster**, the executors live on many machines, and a cluster manager starts them for the driver.

Here there's no cluster. Spark runs in **local mode**: the driver and a single executor share one process on one machine, with 2 cores for tasks. The roles are the same, just in one place. `spark` is the session your program talks to (lesson 3 covers it), and `spark.sparkContext` tells you where Spark is running.

blocks.title: Where is Spark running?
blocks.note: `local[2]` means local mode with 2 cores. `defaultParallelism` is how many tasks Spark plans to run side by side when nothing else decides it: 2 here, one per core. On a cluster it's usually the total number of cores across the executors.

blocks.md: To see how a DataFrame is split, ask for its number of partitions with `df.rdd.getNumPartitions()`. `.rdd` is Spark's lower-level view of the same data (lesson 5 covers it); here it's only used to count partitions.

blocks.title: How many partitions does a table have?
blocks.note: The 12 requests come from one small file, and Spark reads a small file as a single partition. So any step over `api_requests` runs as one task, and the second core has nothing to do.

blocks.title: Asking the DataFrame directly
blocks.note: A DataFrame has no `getNumPartitions` method. The partition count belongs to its lower-level view, so write `api_requests.rdd.getNumPartitions()`.

blocks.md: `df.repartition(n)` gives back a **new** DataFrame with the same rows spread over `n` partitions. The original keeps its partitions. More partitions means more tasks, which lets more cores work at once.

blocks.title: Split a table into more partitions
blocks.code:
spread = api_requests.repartition(4)
print(spread.rdd.getNumPartitions(), "partitions")
print(spread.count(), "requests")
print(api_requests.rdd.getNumPartitions(), "partition in api_requests")
blocks.note: `spread` has 4 partitions, so a step over it becomes 4 tasks, two at a time on 2 cores. It still holds the same 12 requests, and `api_requests` still has its single partition.

blocks.title: More partitions than rows
blocks.note: Spark makes the 10 partitions you asked for even though there are only 4 rows, so at least 6 of them are empty. Each one is still a task to schedule, so more partitions isn't always faster.

blocks.md: Every application also gets an id, `spark.sparkContext.applicationId`. It's different on every run, so we don't print it here. On your own computer or a cluster, Spark also serves a web page (the Spark UI) that lists every job, its stages and their tasks; it's switched off in this environment.

concept.prompt: Spark runs as `local[2]`. Where are the driver and the executor?
choices: On two different machines, one for each
In one process on one machine, with 2 cores for tasks
There's no driver in local mode, only executors
On two executors, one per core
concept.why: In local mode the driver and a single executor share one process on one machine. `[2]` is the number of cores, so 2 tasks can run at once.

concept.prompt: A DataFrame has 6 partitions and Spark has 2 cores. How does one step over it run?
choices: As 1 task, because there is one DataFrame
concept.why: Each partition is one task, so there are 6. With 2 cores, 2 of them run at a time and the rest wait.

choices: Changes `api_requests` so that it has 4 partitions
Gives back a new DataFrame with the same rows in 4 partitions
concept.why: `repartition` returns a new DataFrame with the same rows spread over 4 partitions. `api_requests` keeps its own partitions, and the number of executors doesn't change.

review: The driver runs your program, plans the work and splits it into tasks; executors run the tasks on their cores.
A task is the work for one partition: 6 partitions make 6 tasks, and 2 cores run 2 of them at a time.
Here Spark runs as `local[2]`: the driver and one executor share one process with 2 cores. A cluster spreads executors over many machines.
`spark.sparkContext.master` says where Spark runs, and `spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism` how many tasks it runs side by side by default.
`df.rdd.getNumPartitions()` counts a DataFrame's partitions; a small file is read as one.
`df.repartition(n)` gives back a new DataFrame with the same rows in `n` partitions, even when `n` is more than the number of rows.
